modelCard.title: Model card
modelCard.lead: Answer 5 questions so others understand your model: what it is for, what data it learned from, how good it is and when not to trust it. The card travels with the .lup file and your submission.

purpose.label: 1. What is the model for?
purpose.hint: Example: sorting rubbish into paper, plastic and metal to use the right bin.

data.label: 2. Where does the data come from?
data.hint: Who collected it, where, how many samples? Did you ask permission from people in the photos or recordings?

performance.label: 3. How well does the model work?
performance.hint: Write the accuracy on the Test data and which groups get confused (see the Evaluate step).

limitations.label: 4. When does the model tend to fail?
limitations.hint: Example: dark photos, unusual backgrounds, other accents, ages or skin tones missing from the data.

misuse.label: 5. Do not use this model to…
misuse.hint: Tasks where a wrong guess would harm someone or be unfair to them.

about.title: About & Privacy
about.whatBody: An AI lab that runs entirely in the browser, letting students train machine-learning models and see every step the AI takes with their data.
privacyItems: Images, sounds and text you add are stored only in this browser on this device (IndexedDB).
The site has no server receiving data, no tracking cookies and no analytics.
Only when you press "Export" does your data become a file on your device. You decide who gets it.
Camera and microphone turn on only with your permission and turn off when you leave the page.

inspector.title: Microscope · What does the computer see?
inspector.exactHint: These are exactly the numbers the model receives.
inspector.imageLabel: 224 × 224 image. Click or use arrow keys to pick a pixel.
inspector.howBody: When you add an image, the site crops the largest centred square, resizes it to 224 × 224 pixels and stores it. The numbers here are read directly from that stored image, which is exactly what goes into MobileNetV2. Normalisation uses v / 127.5 − 1, identical to the original training of the model.

represent.title: ③ Represent
represent.leadExplore: Computers do not "see" photos like people. A pre-trained neural network (MobileNetV2) reads the 150,528 numbers of each image and summarises them into 1,280 numbers describing features such as edges, colours, textures and shapes. Similar images get similar numbers.
represent.leadExpert: Transfer learning: MobileNetV2 (α = 0.35, pre-trained on ImageNet, frozen weights) → out_relu layer 7×7×1280 → global average pooling → 1280-dimensional feature vector.
represent.extract: Turn images into vectors ({{count}} not processed)
represent.needTwo: At least 2 images with vectors are needed to draw the map.
represent.mapLead: Each dot is an image. Solid: Train. Ringed: Test. Click a dot to see the image.
represent.mapExactHint: Each dot's position is computed exactly by a linear PCA projection.
represent.mapKept: The map keeps {{percent}}% of the variance of the 1,280 dimensions. The rest is hidden, so dots that look close may not really be close.
represent.wrongLegend: Red ring: the model gets this image wrong (at the selected epoch)
represent.vectorTitle: The 1,280 feature numbers of this image
represent.vectorHint: Each cell is one number: darker means larger. These are exactly the numbers fed into training.

train.title: ④ Train
train.leadExplore: The machine starts by guessing randomly. After each round (epoch) it compares with the answers and nudges its internal numbers so it guesses better next time.
train.leadExpert: Classifier layer: logit = W·x + b (W: {{classes}} × 1280), probability = softmax(logit), cross-entropy loss, Adam optimiser. Glorot initialisation and seeded shuffling make results reproducible.
train.needClasses: At least 2 classes need Train images.
train.replayHint: Drag to see the model at each moment. Epoch 0 is when it still guesses randomly.
train.notSaved: Each training run is recorded in the Experiment log below.
train.stale: Classes changed since the last training. Please train again.

evaluate.title: ⑤ Evaluate
evaluate.testHint: Test set — the more trustworthy score
evaluate.noTest: No Test images yet, so there is no objective score.
evaluate.overfit: The studied score is much higher than the unseen score: the model is memorising rather than understanding (overfitting). Try more varied images.
evaluate.matrixLead: Rows: true class. Columns: predicted class. Diagonal cells are correct. Click a cell to see which images they are.
evaluate.precisionHint: Of the images predicted as this class, the share that is correct
evaluate.recallHint: Of the images that truly belong to this class, the share found

experiments.title: Experiment log
experiments.lead: Every training run is recorded. Select a few to compare, like a scientist keeping lab notes.
experiments.replayHint: Re-run with exactly these settings and seed: the result will be identical.
experiments.changedHint: Images or classes changed after this run, so it cannot be reproduced exactly.
experiments.chartTitle: Test score per epoch for the selected runs
experiments.chartTitleTrain: Train score per epoch for the selected runs
experiments.restored: Restored run {{n}} by re-running with the same seed {{seed}}.
experiments.saveError: Could not save to the log: {{message}}

explain.title: Why did the model predict this?
explain.needModel: Train in step ④ to see explanations.
explain.probabilities: Probability the model computes for each class
explain.heatmapLegend: Red: regions supporting this class · Blue: regions against it
explain.heatmapBadgeHint: Each cell's value is exact, but each cell of the 7×7 grid actually "sees" a larger area than the 32×32-pixel square shaded.
explain.heatmapHowBody: MobileNetV2 divides the image into a 7 × 7 grid; each cell has 1,280 numbers. For the selected class, each cell's score = Σ (class weight × cell number). The mean of the 49 cell scores plus the bias b equals that class's logit exactly — so the map shows exactly how much each cell contributes (the CAM method, identical to Grad-CAM for this model).
explain.heatmapCheck: Check: mean of 49 cells ({{mean}}) + b ({{bias}}) = {{sum}} ≈ logit {{logit}}
explain.pathLead: logit = Σ (feature × weight) + b, then softmax turns logits into probabilities.
explain.pathExactHint: Every number is the real value of the selected model at the current epoch.

threshold.title: Confidence threshold
threshold.lead: Accept an answer only when the model is confident enough; otherwise it answers "Not sure".
threshold.label: Threshold: {{percent}}%
threshold.chart: Answer rate and accuracy by threshold
threshold.tradeoff: A higher threshold means fewer answers but usually more correct ones. In practice (e.g. medicine), "not sure" images should go to a human.

boundary.badgeHint: This is a helper model trained only on the map's 2 axes, so the boundary drawn is exactly its boundary.
boundary.note: The helper model on 2 axes reaches {{acc2d}}% on Train, while the main model (1,280 dimensions) reaches {{accFull}}%. The gap shows how much information the 2D map loses.
boundary.noteNoMain: The helper model on 2 axes reaches {{acc2d}}% on Train.
boundary.needClasses: At least 2 classes need Train images to draw a boundary.

occlusion.title: Cover one cell at a time
occlusion.badgeHint: Each cell is the result of re-running the real model on the image with that cell covered — not an estimate.
occlusion.lead: Cover each cell in grey and let the model guess again. If covering a cell makes the probability drop sharply, the model relies on that region.
occlusion.run: Measure by covering each cell ({{count}} runs)
occlusion.legend: Deep red = covering this cell lowers the probability a lot (important region). Blue = covering it raises the probability.
occlusion.summary: Covering row {{row}}, column {{col}}: probability of "{{name}}" drops from {{from}} to {{to}}.
occlusion.noDrop: Covering any single cell does not lower the probability of "{{name}}" ({{prob}}) — the model does not rely on one region alone.

featureMaps.title: Inside the CNN
featureMaps.badgeHint: Each square shows exactly the numbers one channel of this layer computes for the image, mapped to brightness (min–max per channel).
featureMaps.lead: MobileNet has over 150 layers. Each layer has many channels — each channel is a "filter" that lights up where it recognises a pattern.
featureMaps.shape: {{layer}}: {{h}} × {{w}} cells × {{c}} channels — showing the {{shown}} most active channels

depth.early: Early layer (close to the image): small cells; channels usually respond to strokes, edges and colour patches.
depth.middle: Middle layer: larger cells; channels respond to textures and parts (corners, stripes, curves).
depth.late: Last layer: a 7 × 7 grid with 1280 channels — abstract concepts. Averaging each channel gives exactly the 1280 numbers above.

umap.badgeHint: UMAP only tries to keep "who is close to whom". Distances between clusters, cluster sizes and the axes have no meaning.
umap.lead: UMAP arranges images so that images close together in 1280 dimensions stay close on the map. Clusters are often clearer than PCA, but this is a non-linear transformation.
umap.needMore: UMAP needs at least {{count}} images with features.
umap.note: UMAP with seed {{seed}}: the same data always gives the same map. Read only "who is close to whom"; do not measure distances.

playground.title: Algorithm Playground
playground.lead: Six core machine-learning algorithms on 2-D data so every step is visible. Written from scratch in TypeScript and cross-checked against scikit-learn.

knn.name: k-nearest neighbours (k-NN)
knn.summary: A new point takes the majority label of its k closest points.
knn.concept: neighbours · distance · small vs large k
knn.intro: k-NN learns no formula: it memorises all the data, then for each new point finds the k closest points (Euclidean distance) and lets them vote.
knn.exactHint: Coloured regions are the real k-NN result at the centre of each cell of a 30×30 grid; votes are real counts.

decision-tree.name: Decision tree
decision-tree.summary: A chain of yes/no questions cuts the plane into rectangles.
decision-tree.intro: At each node the computer tries every possible threshold on every feature and picks the question that makes the child groups purest (lowest Gini or entropy). Press "Grow one node" to watch the tree grow.
decision-tree.exactHint: Coloured regions are the tree's real predictions at the centre of each cell of a 40×40 grid; thresholds, sample counts and impurity are real numbers.

linear-regression.name: Linear regression
linear-regression.summary: Drag a line yourself, then compare it with the computer's line by squared error.
linear-regression.intro: The model is a line ŷ = w·x + b. "Good" means a small mean squared error (MSE). Each square's side is one error: the smaller the total area, the better the line.
linear-regression.exactHint: MSE, the computer's line (least-squares solution) and the gradient-descent step are all real calculations.

gradient-descent.name: Gradient descent
gradient-descent.summary: A ball rolls downhill on the loss surface; steps that are too long fly off.
gradient-descent.intro: The gradient ∇f points in the steepest uphill direction. Each step moves against it by an amount proportional to the learning rate η. This is how neural networks are trained.
gradient-descent.exactHint: The surface has an exact formula and derivative; every dot on the path is a real computed step.

k-means.name: k-means clustering
k-means.summary: No labels: cluster centres move until they stop.
k-means.intro: k-means repeats two things: assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points. The computer does not know the true labels, so the colours are clusters it found, not answers.
k-means.exactHint: Each frame is a real step of Lloyd's algorithm; starting centres come from seeded k-means++.

neural-network.name: Mini neural network
neural-network.summary: Add hidden layers to separate data that no straight line can.
neural-network.intro: Each hidden neuron computes a weighted sum and passes it through an activation function. Combined, neurons can draw curved boundaries. Trained with gradient descent and backpropagation.
neural-network.exactHint: Coloured regions and per-neuron maps are the network's real outputs at each grid-cell centre; loss is the real mean cross-entropy.

common.addHint: Click the plot to add a point of the selected class.

knn.plotLabel: Data plane; coloured regions are the class k-NN predicts with k = {{k}}
knn.kHint: Small k: jagged boundary, easily fooled by one stray point. Large k: smooth boundary, but small classes get outvoted.
knn.probeHint: Click the plot to place the point to classify; dashed lines connect it to its k nearest neighbours.
knn.verdict: The point is predicted as Class {{n}} ({{votes}}/{{k}} votes).
knn.tieRule: On a tie, the class with the smaller number wins (same as scikit-learn).

tree.plotLabel: Data plane; coloured regions are the class the decision tree predicts
tree.overfitHint: Deeper trees memorise the training set (solid line rises), but the test set (dashed) can drop: that is overfitting.

regression.plotLabel: Data points, your line (orange) and the computer's line (teal)
regression.clickHint: Click the plot to add points. Vertical segments are each point's error.
regression.gdStep: Let the computer fix one step (gradient descent, η = {{lr}})
regression.machineLine: Computer's line: ŷ = {{w}}·x + ({{b}}). No straight line has a smaller MSE on this data.
regression.mseHint: MSE = mean of (y − ŷ)². Squaring punishes one big error much more than several small ones.

gradient.plotLabel: Contour map of the loss surface {{formula}}; darker is lower
gradient.clickHint: Click the plot to choose a starting point. ✕ marks the global minimum.
gradient.diverged: The ball is higher than where it started: η is so large that each step jumps over the bottom and climbs higher.
gradient.lossChart: Value of f at each step
gradient.viewNote: The surface is seen from above (a contour map), like a topographic map.

kmeans.plotLabel: Unlabelled data points and {{k}} cluster centres
kmeans.unsupervisedNote: The data has no labels. Try "Two nested circles" to see that k-means only finds round blob-shaped clusters.
kmeans.initNote: Starting centres chosen by k-means++ (seed {{seed}}). A different start can give a different result.

phases.init: Start: place k centres. No point belongs to a cluster yet.
phases.assign: Assign: each point joins its nearest centre.
phases.update: Move: each centre moves to the mean of its cluster's points (dashed arrow).

kmeans.inertia: Sum of squared distances to centres = {{value}}
kmeans.converged: The centres no longer move: the algorithm stops (converged).
kmeans.inertiaHint: The sum of squared distances never increases between iterations, so the algorithm is guaranteed to stop.

neural.plotLabel: Data plane; coloured regions are the class the network predicts (darker = more confident)
neural.neuronsHint: Each neuron's output over the whole plane: orange is positive, blue negative, pale near 0.
neural.fullBatchNote: Each step uses all the data to compute the gradient (full-batch gradient descent). Try 1 neuron on "Two nested circles": the network can only draw a straight line.

tabular.lead: Teach the computer to predict one column of a table from the others. At every step you can see what it does with the numbers.

steps.check: Choose columns and check the data
steps.represent: Representation: how the computer sees the table

data.empty: Pick a sample dataset, upload a CSV file or paste a table from Excel / Google Sheets. Data stays on this device only.
data.uploadHint: The first row holds column names. Separated by commas, semicolons or tabs. At most {{rows}} rows, {{columns}} columns.

csvErrors.too-large: The file is too large (about 2 MB at most).
csvErrors.too-many-rows: The table has {{detail}} rows, over the {{maxRows}}-row limit.
csvErrors.too-many-columns: The table has {{detail}} columns, over the {{maxColumns}}-column limit.
csvErrors.unclosed-quote: A quote opened on line {{line}} is never closed.
csvErrors.ragged-row: Line {{line}} has a different number of cells from the header ({{detail}}).
csvErrors.empty-header: Column {{detail}} has no name in the header row.

taskHint.classification: The computer predicts which value of the label column each row belongs to.
taskHint.regression: The computer predicts a number; the error is the distance to the true number.

setup.testRatio: Share kept aside as the test set

prepareErrors.no-features: Choose at least one feature column other than the label.
prepareErrors.target-not-numeric: Regression needs a numeric label column.
prepareErrors.too-many-classes: The label column has {{count}} different values, too many to classify (at most 10). If it is a number, choose Regression.
prepareErrors.single-class: The label column has only one value: there is nothing to tell apart.
prepareErrors.too-many-categories: Column "{{column}}" has {{count}} different text values (at most 20). Untick this column.
prepareErrors.too-few-rows: Only {{count}} usable rows remain; at least 10 are needed.

quality.title: Data check assistant
quality.dropped-rows: {{count}} rows were dropped because the label or a chosen feature is missing.
quality.imbalance: Imbalance: class "{{smallest}}" has only {{smallestCount}} rows while "{{largest}}" has {{largestCount}}. The computer may predict "{{smallest}}" less often.
quality.id-like: Column "{{column}}" has almost one value per row, like an ID. The computer would memorise IDs instead of learning a pattern: better untick it.
quality.constant: Column "{{column}}" has a single value, so it cannot help tell rows apart.
quality.small-data: Only {{count}} rows: test results will vary a lot between splits.

represent.mapHint: Each dot is a real row, placed by the standardised values of the two chosen columns.
represent.plotLabel: Scatter plot of the two chosen columns
represent.axisNote: Axis units are "standard deviations from the mean". Points beyond 3.5 are drawn at the edge.
represent.needNumeric: At least two numeric columns are needed to draw the map.
represent.tableHint: Exactly the numbers the model receives for this row.
represent.tableCaption: Row {{row}} of the table (first row of the training set)
represent.whyScale: Standardising lets columns with different units (mm, g…) be compared fairly. k-NN and logistic regression use standardised numbers; decision trees and linear regression use original numbers so thresholds and coefficients read in real units.

tree.name: Decision tree
tree.how: A chain of "column ≤ threshold?" questions chosen by the computer.

logistic.name: Logistic regression
logistic.how: Adds up columns times weights into a score for each class, then turns scores into probabilities.

knn.name: k-nearest neighbours
knn.how: Finds the k most similar rows in the training set and takes the majority label.

linear.name: Linear regression
linear.how: Prediction = intercept + sum of (coefficient × column value).

knn-regression.name: k-nearest neighbours
knn-regression.how: Averages the values of the k most similar training rows.

model.cHint: Small C: weights are pulled towards 0 (simpler model). Large C: the model follows the training data more closely.
model.kHint: Distances are computed on the standardised columns.
model.linearNoSettings: Linear regression has nothing to tune: the computer directly solves for the least-squares answer.
model.stale: The data or settings changed: press Train to update the results.

evaluate.confusion: Confusion matrix on the test set
evaluate.overfit: Training accuracy is much higher than test accuracy: the model may be memorising (overfitting).
evaluate.regressionHint: R² = 1 means every prediction is right; 0 means no better than always guessing the mean. RMSE is a typical error, in the same unit as "{{target}}".
evaluate.predVsTrue: True value (horizontal) and predicted value (vertical) on the test set; the diagonal is a perfect prediction
evaluate.explainHint: Weights, thresholds and importances are the real numbers of the model just trained.
evaluate.importances: Importance of each column (total impurity decrease)
evaluate.logisticBinary: Weights apply to standardised columns. A positive weight pushes the prediction towards "{{cls}}", a negative one away from it.
evaluate.logisticMulti: Each class has its own weights (on standardised columns). The class with the highest total score wins.
evaluate.linearHint: Each coefficient says how much the prediction changes when that column grows by 1 unit and the others stay the same. A coefficient is not a cause-and-effect relationship.
evaluate.knnHint: k-NN learns no weights: it remembers the {{n}} training rows and, for each prediction, finds the {{k}} closest ones.

use.invalid: Fill in every cell; number cells must be numbers (a decimal comma is fine).
use.neighbors: {{k}} closest rows in the training set:

colab.title: Keep learning with Python: a Google Colab notebook

colab.imageDescription: Download a notebook holding the 1,280 feature numbers of each image (not the images themselves); it retrains the classifier layer with Keras and converts the complete model to TensorFlow Lite.

colab.done: Notebook created ({{size}} MB). Check your Downloads folder.
colab.large: The notebook is fairly large, so Colab may open it slowly.
colab.privacy: The notebook is created on this device. LUP Machine sends no data anywhere; only if you upload the notebook to Colab yourself does its data live in your Google Drive.
colab.textDescription: Download a notebook that rebuilds exactly this vocabulary and model with scikit-learn, on the same sentences and the same training / test split, then compares the results with LUP Machine.
colab.audioDescription: Download a notebook holding the 160 feature numbers of each clip (not the audio itself) that rebuilds the same model with scikit-learn on the same training / test split, then compares the results with LUP Machine.

text.lead: Teach the computer to classify Vietnamese sentences. At every step you can see how a sentence becomes numbers and which words led to the prediction.

data.empty: Pick a sample set, type sentences for each group yourself, or upload a CSV file. Data stays on this device only.
data.writeHint: Name each group and type one sentence per line.
data.uploadHint: A CSV file with one column of sentences and one column of labels (first row holds column names).
data.needTwoColumns: The table needs at least two columns: one for sentences and one for labels.

editor.nameError: Each group needs its own name; names cannot be empty or repeated.

prepareErrors.too-few-sentences: Only {{count}} usable sentences; at least 6 are needed.
prepareErrors.single-class: At least two different groups are needed.
prepareErrors.too-many-classes: There are {{count}} groups, too many (at most 10). Check the label column.

quality.dropped: {{count}} sentences were dropped because they are empty or have no label.
quality.imbalance: Imbalance: group "{{smallest}}" has only {{smallestCount}} sentences while "{{largest}}" has {{largestCount}}.
quality.few-examples: Group "{{label}}" has only {{count}} sentences; at least 5 are recommended.
quality.duplicates: {{count}} sentences are duplicates (ignoring case and punctuation).
quality.conflict: The sentence "{{text}}" appears in several groups ({{labels}}): the computer would be taught two opposite answers.
quality.short: {{count}} sentences are very short (under 3 syllables) and carry almost no information.

represent.title: Microscope: one sentence as a vector
represent.exactHint: Exactly the syllables, counts and TF-IDF values the model uses for this sentence.
represent.sentence: Sentence to inspect (feel free to edit)
represent.unknown: Not in the training vocabulary, so ignored: {{words}}
represent.vectorSize: The sentence vector has {{total}} cells (one per vocabulary word); only {{nonzero}} are non-zero.
represent.tfidfHint: idf = ln((1 + {{n}}) / (1 + training sentences containing the word)) + 1: words found in many sentences (like "và", "là") get a small idf. TF-IDF = count × idf, then divided by the vector length.
represent.frequentTitle: Most frequent syllables in each group (training set)
represent.frequentHint: Frequent does not mean useful: a word common to every group does not tell groups apart.

naive-bayes.name: Naive Bayes
naive-bayes.how: Counts which group each word tends to appear in, then multiplies the probabilities (adds logs).

logistic.name: Logistic regression
logistic.how: Each word has a weight per group; weight × TF-IDF adds up to a score, then scores become probabilities.

model.alphaHint: Adds α to every word count so a word never seen in a group does not make the probability zero.

evaluate.topTitle: Most characteristic words of each group
evaluate.topHint: Ranked by the actual weights / probabilities of the model just trained.
evaluate.topNb: Ranked by log P(word | group) minus the average over groups: words at the top lean most towards that group.
evaluate.topLogistic: Ranked by the word's weight for that group (with 3 or more groups: minus the average over groups).

use.noKnownWords: No word of this sentence is in the vocabulary: the prediction only reflects the group proportions seen in training.
use.whyHint: The numbers are the model's real calculation; they add up exactly to the group's score.
use.colorLegend: Green: the syllable pushes the sentence towards "{{cls}}". Red: pulls it away. Darker means stronger. No colour: unknown word.
use.tableCaption: Score of "{{cls}}" relative to the average over groups
use.totalHint: The group with the highest total score is chosen.
use.totalHintBinary: With 2 groups: a positive score leans towards this group, a negative one towards the other.

audio.lead: Teach the computer to recognise sounds. At every step you can see how sound becomes numbers: waveform → frequency spectrum → mel spectrogram → 160 numbers.

data.empty: No sound groups yet. Add a group below, then record with the microphone or upload files, or use the sample sounds.
data.loadSamples: Use sample sounds: bell / whistle / drum
data.samplesNote: The sample sounds are generated by formulas (16 clips per group), not real recordings.
data.confirmDeleteClass: Delete group "{{name}}" and all its clips?
data.unsupported: This browser does not support Web Audio, so sound cannot be recorded or read. Please use a recent Chrome or Edge.
data.privacy: Sounds are stored only on this device as 1-second, 16 kHz clips; original files are not kept and nothing is sent anywhere.

live.hint: Live spectrum computed by the browser (different window and resolution), only to show the microphone is listening; the model does not use it.

quality.silent: {{count}} clips are almost silent: the microphone may be off or too far away.
quality.clipped: {{count}} clips are distorted because they are too loud (hit the microphone's maximum).
quality.few-clips: Group "{{label}}" has only {{count}} clips; at least 5 are recommended.
quality.imbalance: Imbalance: group "{{smallest}}" has only {{smallestCount}} clips while "{{largest}}" has {{largestCount}}.

prepareErrors.single-class: Sounds from at least two groups are needed.
prepareErrors.too-few-samples: Only {{count}} clips; at least 6 are needed to train.

inspector.exactHint: Exactly the calculations the model uses: same frames, Hann window, FFT, mel filters and pooling.
inspector.waveHint: The microphone measures air pressure {{rate}} times per second: 1 second is {{n}} numbers. The yellow area is the frame being viewed.
inspector.fftTitle: ② Frequency spectrum of one frame (FFT)
inspector.fftHint: Take {{win}} samples (25 ms), multiply by a Hann window to soften both ends, then use the fast Fourier transform (FFT, {{nfft}} points) to find which frequencies the frame contains: {{bins}} values from 0 to 8 kHz.
inspector.melLabel: Mel spectrogram: horizontal axis is time, vertical axis is frequency band
inspector.melHint: Repeat step ② for all {{frames}} frames (10 ms apart), group frequencies into {{bands}} mel bands (from about {{low}} Hz to {{high}} Hz; low bands are narrow and high bands wide, like human hearing) and convert to decibels. Brighter is louder. Dashed lines split 4 time segments.
inspector.poolTitle: ④ The 160 numbers the model receives
inspector.poolLabel: Average loudness of each band in each time segment
inspector.poolHint: Average each mel band within {{segments}} time segments: {{bands}} × {{segments}} = {{total}} numbers. Columns are time segments (left to right), rows are frequency bands (low at the bottom).

logistic.name: Logistic regression
logistic.how: Each of the 160 cells has a weight per group; they add up to a score that becomes a probability. Readable back as a map of important spectrum regions.

knn.name: k-nearest neighbours
knn.how: Finds the k most similar training clips (distance in dB) and takes the majority group.

model.kHint: Distances use the original dB values, not standardised: standardising would amplify the noise in silent cells.

evaluate.importanceHint: The model's real weights arranged as a 40-band × 4-segment grid.
evaluate.importanceLegend: Orange: louder than average in that cell pushes towards this group. Blue: pulls away. Rows are frequency bands (low at the bottom), columns are time segments.
evaluate.knnNoMap: k-NN learns no weights, so there is no such map; see the neighbours in step ⑥.

use.empty: Record 1 second or upload an audio file to try.
use.whyHint: Contribution = the cell's standardised value × weight; together with the fixed part they add up exactly to the group's score.
use.contributionHint: Score of "{{cls}}" relative to the average over groups = {{base}} (fixed part) + sum of cells = {{total}}. Orange pushes towards this group, blue pulls away.
use.knnHint: Press ▶ to hear the most similar training clips the computer relied on.

pose.lead: Teach the computer to recognise body poses or hand gestures. A detection model finds the joint coordinates; only those numbers are stored and used for learning — no images are kept.

camera.handScore: Probability of a hand in the frame: {{score}}%

state.loading-model: Loading the detection model (needs internet the first time)…
state.denied: Camera access is not allowed. Click the lock icon in the address bar to allow it.
state.unavailable: No camera found on this device.
state.model-error: Could not load the detection model. Check the internet connection and try again.

kindHint.body: MoveNet finds 17 joints (nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles). Stand far enough from the camera to show your whole body.
kindHint.hand: The hand model finds 21 points (wrist and 4 points on each finger). Put your hand inside the square in the middle of the camera.

data.kindLocked: The project already has samples, so the kind cannot change.
data.empty: No groups yet. Add a group below, then turn on the camera to record poses, upload photos, or use the sample poses.

loadSamples.body: Use sample poses: arms up / arms out / hands on hips / standing straight
loadSamples.hand: Use sample gestures: open hand / fist / V sign

data.samplesNote: The samples are generated by formulas (simulated joint coordinates, 15 per group); there are no photos of real people.
data.handGuide: Put your hand inside the dashed square; the model only looks there.
data.thumb: Skeleton of one sample of group {{name}}
data.confirmDeleteClass: Delete group "{{name}}" and all its pose samples?
data.privacy: Only joint coordinates are stored on this device; photos and camera frames are not saved and nothing is sent anywhere.

quality.unusable: {{count}} samples cannot be used because the shoulders and hips (or wrist and middle-finger knuckle) are not clearly visible.
quality.missing-joints: {{count}} samples miss many joints (for example the legs are out of the frame).
quality.few-poses: Group "{{label}}" has only {{count}} samples; at least 5 are recommended.
quality.imbalance: Imbalance: group "{{smallest}}" has only {{smallestCount}} samples while "{{largest}}" has {{largestCount}}.

prepareErrors.too-few-samples: Only {{count}} usable samples; at least 6 are needed.
prepareErrors.single-class: Samples from at least two groups are needed.

inspector.exactHint: Exactly the coordinates the detection model found and the normalisation the learning model uses.
inspector.rawTitle: ① Joint coordinates in the frame

rawHint.body: Frame of {{w}} × {{h}} pixels. The orange circle is the new origin (between the hips); the orange segment is "1 unit" (hips → shoulders).
rawHint.hand: Frame of {{w}} × {{h}} pixels. The orange circle is the new origin (wrist); the orange segment is "1 unit" (wrist → middle-finger knuckle).

inspector.normLabel: Skeleton after moving the origin and changing the unit

normHint.body: The origin moves to between the hips and lengths are measured in torso lengths, so standing near or far, left or right gives the same numbers.
normHint.hand: The origin moves to the wrist and lengths are measured in palm sizes, so a hand near or far from the camera gives the same numbers.

cannotNormalize.body: This sample does not clearly show the shoulders and hips, so it cannot be normalised; the model will skip it.
cannotNormalize.hand: This sample does not clearly show the wrist and middle-finger knuckle, so it cannot be normalised; the model will skip it.

inspector.tableCaption: {{n}} joints × 2 coordinates = {{dims}} numbers the model receives
inspector.tableHint: Joints with confidence below {{min}} (faded) count as not clearly visible and are set to 0.

logistic.name: Logistic regression
logistic.how: Each coordinate has a weight per group; they add up to a score that becomes a probability. Readable back as the importance of each joint.

knn.name: k-nearest neighbours
knn.how: Finds the k training samples whose joints are closest and takes the majority group.

model.kHint: Distances use normalised coordinates (units: torso length / hand size).

evaluate.importanceTitle: Which joints does the model look at?
evaluate.importanceHint: Joint importance = |weight of x| + |weight of y|, from the model's real weights.
evaluate.importanceLabel: Importance of the joints for group {{cls}}
evaluate.importanceLegend: Drawn on the average pose of each group; the bigger the dot, the more that joint affects the group's score.
evaluate.knnNoMap: k-NN learns no weights, so there is no such picture; see the neighbours in step ⑥.

use.empty: Turn on the camera or upload a photo to try.
use.whyHint: A joint's contribution = (normalised value × weight) for x plus for y; all joints plus the fixed part add up exactly to the group's score.
use.contributionHint: On the skeleton: orange joints push towards "{{cls}}", blue ones pull away; bigger dots matter more. Score relative to the average over groups = {{base}} (fixed part) + sum over joints = {{total}}.
use.neighbors: The {{k}} closest training samples belong to: {{labels}}.
